From ABC to Effective Roth and Ridout Constants for Cubic Roots

Karsten Müller    Michael Taktikos
February 2026, final version
Abstract

Enrico Bombieri showed conditionally (1994) that the ABC conjecture implies Roth’s theorem, and Van Frankenhuysen (1999) later provided a complete proof. Building on Bombieri’s and Van der Poorten’s explicit formula for continued-fraction coefficients of algebraic numbers—specialized to cubic roots—we derive an effective bound for a Roth-type constant assuming an effective form of ABC. Roth’s original argument establishes existence but does not yield an explicit value; our approach makes the dependence on the ABC parameters explicit and also gives an explicit bound in the corresponding special case of Ridout’s theorem.

We then introduce the notion of approximation gain as a refinement of the “quality” of an abc-triple. For c in a large computational range (verified up to c<263c<2^{63}), the approximation gain remains below a strikingly small threshold, motivating the conjecture that the approximation gain is always smaller than 32\frac{3}{2}. This suggests a potential strategy for attacking ABC by bounding approximation gain and power gain separately. 11 1 The authors are grateful to Benne de Weger, Joshua Lampert, Timm Lampert, Enrico Bombieri, Machiel van Frankenhuysen, Wadim Zudilin, Michel Waldschmidt, Preda Mihailescu, Paul Vojta, Stephane Fischler, Robin Zhang, Abderrahmane Nitaj, Sam Chow, Noah Lebowitz-Lockard, Ingo Althöfer, David Broadhurst, Ulrich Tamm and ChatGPT.

1 Introduction

Roth’s theorem is famously deep, and its original proof is both long and ineffective (see Roth (1955)). In particular, it guarantees the existence of a constant in the Diophantine approximation bound, but it does not provide an explicit value or a practical way to compute one.

Bombieri proved conditionally in 1994 that Roth’s theorem follows from the ABC conjecture, and Van Frankenhuysen later gave a full proof in 1999 (Van Frankenhuysen (1999)). In this paper we revisit that implication with an additional goal: making the constants explicit in a natural family of cases. We focus on cubic roots and use an explicit continued-fraction formula of Bombieri and Van der Poorten (Bombieri & Van der Poorten (1975)) for the coefficients of regular continued fractions of algebraic numbers. This yields a concrete relationship between the ε\varepsilon-parameters in Roth-type inequalities and the corresponding ε\varepsilon in ABC, and it leads to an explicit upper bound for the inverse of the Roth constant in our setting.

In our earlier paper (Sibbertsen (2022)), we showed that a weakened form of ABC follows from Roth’s theorem in certain special cases. The present work uses essentially the same vocabulary and techniques, but in the opposite direction: assuming (an effective form of) ABC, we extract explicit Diophantine approximation bounds.

We also introduce the approximation gain, which is always lower or equal to the quality of an ABC hit.

2 Approximation gains for ABC

2.1 Roth’s theorem

In the following, the coefficients of the regular continued fraction are called bnb_{n} and the approximants pnqn\frac{p_{n}}{q_{n}}.

Theorem 2.1.

Roth’s Theorem: Let aa be an algebraic number. Then for every ε>0\varepsilon>0, there exists a constant C dependent on the algebraic number aa and ε\varepsilon such that for all positive integers pp and qq:

|a−pq|>Cq2+ε.\Large|a-\frac{p}{q}|>\frac{C}{q^{2+\varepsilon}}. (2.1)
Proof.

See Roth (1955). ∎

Van Frankenhuysen (1999) discusses Roth’s Theorem and its implication by the ABC conjecture in detail and investigates effective versions of Mordell’s conjecture. Furthermore, Granville and Tucker (2002, p.1229) show that a generalized version of Roth’s theorem implies the ABC conjecture effectively.

With the help of the inequality for regular continued fractions from this follows bn+1≤qnεCb_{n+1}\leq\frac{q_{n}^{\varepsilon}}{C}

2.2 Formula by Bombieri and Van der Poorten

Our main technical input is the explicit formula of Bombieri and Van der Poorten for the continued-fraction coefficients of algebraic numbers by (Bombieri & Van der Poorten, 1975, p.151, Theorem 3, formula (13)), in whichf⁡(x){f(x)} is the minimal polynomial of the algebraic number.

The formula links two quantities—call them dnd_{n} and bnb_{n} — and is therefore well suited to bridge ABC-type information (which naturally arises from integer identities involving dnd_{n} with Diophantine approximation data encoded by bnb_{n}).

f′​(x)f⁡(x)\frac{f^{\prime}(x)}{f(x)} leads to dnd_{n} in the denominator. This holds because f′​(x)f⁡(x)\frac{f^{\prime}(x)}{f(x)} results in f′​(pnqn)f⁡(pnqn)=qns​s​pns−1dn​qns−1\frac{f^{\prime}(\frac{p_{n}}{q_{n}})}{f(\frac{p_{n}}{q_{n}})}=\frac{q_{n}^{s}sp_{n}^{s-1}}{d_{n}q_{n}^{s-1}} for the convergents with f⁡(x)=xs−kf(x)=x^{s}-k being the minimal polynomial of the ssth root of k.

For cubic roots α=k3>1\alpha=\sqrt[3]{k}>1 with minimal polynomial f⁡(x)=x3−kf(x)=x^{3}-k, the Bombieri–Van der Poorten formula for the continued-fraction coefficients reads

bn+1=qn3​f′​(pn/qn)f⁡(pn/qn)+Rn,\Large b_{n+1}=\frac{q_{n}^{3}f^{\prime}(p_{n}/q_{n})}{f(p_{n}/q_{n})}+R_{n},

where pn/qnp_{n}/q_{n} are the convergents and RnR_{n} is the remainder. Evaluating the derivative gives the leading term

3​pn2​qndn,dn=|pn3−k​qn3|.\Large\frac{3p_{n}^{2}q_{n}}{d_{n}},\hskip 14.40004ptd_{n}=|p_{n}^{3}-kq_{n}^{3}|.

A simple estimate of RnR_{n} using |α−pn/qn|<1/qn2|\alpha-p_{n}/q_{n}|<1/q_{n}^{2} shows that |Rn|≤3​pn​qn3/dn|R_{n}|\leq 3p_{n}q_{n}^{3}/d_{n}. For all convergents with pn>qnp_{n}>q_{n}, which holds for all but possibly the first, the leading term strictly dominates the remainder. Consequently, the inequality

bn+1≤3​pn2​qndn\Large b_{n+1}\leq\frac{3p_{n}^{2}q_{n}}{d_{n}}

holds rigorously, and the error term can be safely ignored. No additional constant depending on kk is required.

For quartic roots α=k4\alpha=\sqrt[4]{k}, the formula may fail for the first few convergents, but for each fixed kk it becomes valid from some sufficiently large convergent onward.

2.3 ABC Conjecture

To formulate the ABC Conjecture we need the following definition:

Definition 2.2.

For a positive integer aa, r​a​d​(a)rad(a) is the product of the distinct prime factors of aa.

Definition 2.3 (ABC Conjecture).

For every positive real number ε\varepsilon, there exists a constant KεK_{\varepsilon} such that for all triples (a,b,c)(a,b,c) of coprime positive integers, with a+b=ca+b=c:

c<Kε⋅r​a​d​(a​b​c)1+ε.\Large c<K_{\varepsilon}\cdot rad(abc)^{1+\varepsilon}.

Note that this version of the ABC Conjecture is not effective. This is so because only the existence of a constant KεK_{\varepsilon} is claimed without specifying how to calculate KεK_{\varepsilon} for given ϵ\epsilon.

2.4 Resulting ABC equations

We consider the convergents (pn/qn)(p_{n}/q_{n}) of the regular continued fraction of k3\sqrt[3]{k}, which satisfy the “resulting equation”

pn3=k​qn3+dn,\Large p_{n}^{3}=kq_{n}^{3}+d_{n},

with integers pn,qn,dnp_{n},q_{n},d_{n} and gcd⁡(pn,qn)=1\gcd(p_{n},q_{n})=1.

To apply the ABC conjecture, we define

gn:=gcd⁡(k​qn3,dn)\Large g_{n}:=\gcd(kq_{n}^{3},d_{n})

and consider the triple

(pn3gn,k​qn3gn,dngn),\Large\left(\frac{p_{n}^{3}}{g_{n}},\frac{kq_{n}^{3}}{g_{n}},\frac{d_{n}}{g_{n}}\right),

which will be coprime.

Using the resulting equation, we have

gn=gcd⁡(k​qn3,dn)=gcd⁡(k​qn3,pn3−k​qn3)=gcd⁡(k​qn3,pn3).\Large g_{n}=\gcd(kq_{n}^{3},d_{n})=\gcd(kq_{n}^{3},p_{n}^{3}-kq_{n}^{3})=\gcd(kq_{n}^{3},p_{n}^{3}).

Since gcd⁡(pn,qn)=1\gcd(p_{n},q_{n})=1, it follows that gcd⁡(pn3,qn3)=1\gcd(p_{n}^{3},q_{n}^{3})=1, and therefore

gn=gcd⁡(k,pn3)≤k.\Large g_{n}=\gcd(k,p_{n}^{3})\leq k.

Thus gn≥1g_{n}\geq 1 and gn≤kg_{n}\leq k, giving an explicit bound. Dividing by gng_{n} ensures that the resulting ABC triple is coprime, as required for the application of the ABC conjecture.

2.5 Construction of the effective bound for the inverse of Roth’s constant

Let (pn/qn)(p_{n}/q_{n}) be the convergents of k3\sqrt[3]{k}, with the resulting equation

pn3=k​qn3+dn,gcd⁡(pn,qn)=1,\Large p_{n}^{3}=kq_{n}^{3}+d_{n},\hskip 14.40004pt\gcd(p_{n},q_{n})=1,

and define

gn:=gcd⁡(k​qn3,dn)=gcd⁡(k,pn3)≤k.\Large g_{n}:=\gcd(kq_{n}^{3},d_{n})=\gcd(k,p_{n}^{3})\leq k.

Dividing through by gng_{n} gives a coprime ABC triple

(pn3gn,k​qn3gn,dngn),\Large\left(\frac{p_{n}^{3}}{g_{n}},\frac{kq_{n}^{3}}{g_{n}},\frac{d_{n}}{g_{n}}\right),

so the effective ABC conjecture yields

pn3gn≤Kε​Rad​(pn3gn⋅k​qn3gn⋅dngn)1+ε.\Large\frac{p_{n}^{3}}{g_{n}}\leq K_{\varepsilon}\,\mathrm{Rad}\left(\frac{p_{n}^{3}}{g_{n}}\cdot\frac{kq_{n}^{3}}{g_{n}}\cdot\frac{d_{n}}{g_{n}}\right)^{1+\varepsilon}.

Multiplying both sides by gng_{n}, we obtain

pn3≤Kε​gn1−(1+ε)⋅3​Rad​(pn​qn​dn​k)1+ε.\Large p_{n}^{3}\leq K_{\varepsilon}\,g_{n}^{1-(1+\varepsilon)\cdot 3}\,\mathrm{Rad}\big(p_{n}q_{n}d_{n}k\big)^{1+\varepsilon}.

Since gn≤kg_{n}\leq k, we can bound

gn1−(1+ε)⋅3≤k1−3​(1+ε).\Large g_{n}^{1-(1+\varepsilon)\cdot 3}\leq k^{1-3(1+\varepsilon)}.

Next, using Bombieri–Van der Poorten’s explicit formula for the continued-fraction coefficients in the cubic case, we have

dn≤3​pn2qn​bn+1.\Large d_{n}\leq\frac{3p_{n}^{2}}{q_{n}b_{n+1}}.

Substituting into the ABC inequality gives

bn+1≤Kε11+ε​ 3​k​pn3​ε1+ε​gn1/(1+ε)qn.\Large b_{n+1}\leq K_{\varepsilon}^{\frac{1}{1+\varepsilon}}\,3k\,p_{n}^{\frac{3\varepsilon}{1+\varepsilon}}\frac{g_{n}^{1/(1+\varepsilon)}}{q_{n}}.

Finally, Roth’s theorem implies the existence of a constant CC, depending only on εRoth\varepsilon_{\mathrm{Roth}} and k3\sqrt[3]{k}, such that

bn+1≤qnεRothC.\Large b_{n+1}\leq\frac{q_{n}^{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{Roth}}}}{C}.

Comparing the two bounds for bn+1b_{n+1}, we get the relationship between the epsilons:

εRoth=3​εABC1+εABC,\Large\varepsilon_{\mathrm{Roth}}=3\frac{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ABC}}}{1+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ABC}}},

and an explicit bound for the inverse of Roth’s constant:

1C≤Kε11+ε​ 3​k​(pnqn)3​ε1+ε.\Large\frac{1}{C}\leq K_{\varepsilon}^{\frac{1}{1+\varepsilon}}\,3k\,\left(\frac{p_{n}}{q_{n}}\right)^{\frac{3\varepsilon}{1+\varepsilon}}.

Since gn≤kg_{n}\leq k and pnqn≤p1q1\frac{p_{n}}{q_{n}}\leq\frac{p_{1}}{q_{1}} in this case, this provides a fully explicit ABC-based bound for the inverse of Roth’s constant.

2.11 An explicit bound for Ridout’s theorem

Using the ABC method it is also possible to give an explicit bound for the number of solutions of Ridout’s theorem for the special case of the approximants of the regular continued fraction:

Theorem 2.4.

(D. Ridout, 1957):

Let S be a finite set of prime numbers. For any real algebraic number a, for any ε>0\varepsilon>0, the set of pq\frac{p}{q} with p an integer and q a S–integer and

∣a−pq∣<q−1−ε\Large\mid a-\frac{p}{q}\mid<{q^{-1-\varepsilon}}

is finite.

See Waldschmidt (2008) page 75.

As we are dealing with the prime factorisation, here the squares roots are interesting as well and a bound follows from ABC as follows:

For k\sqrt{k} the resulting equations are

pn2=k​qn2+dnp_{n}^{2}=kq_{n}^{2}+d_{n}

resp

k​qn2=pn2+dnkq_{n}^{2}=p_{n}^{2}+d_{n}

and so with R​a​d​(qn)Rad(q_{n}) given as qnq_{n} is an S integer we get the bound

pn1−ε≤Kε​R​a​d​(qn)1+ε​dn1+ε​k1+ε{p_{n}^{1-\varepsilon}}\leq K_{\varepsilon}Rad(q_{n})^{1+\varepsilon}d_{n}^{1+\varepsilon}k^{1+\varepsilon}

for the pnp_{n} and so the number of solutions must be finite and an explicit bound is given, which follows from an explicit ABC version.

2.13 Generalization of Ridout’s Theorem to All S-Integers

Let a=ka=\sqrt{k} be a positive square-free integer and let SS be a finite set of primes. Consider solutions (p,q)(p,q) with p∈ℤp\in\mathbb{Z}, q∈ℤSq\in\mathbb{Z}_{S} (an SS-integer) satisfying

|a−pq|<q−1−ε.\Large\left|a-\frac{p}{q}\right|<q^{-1-\varepsilon}.

Define the “error term”

d=|p2−k​q2|.\Large d=|p^{2}-kq^{2}|.

To apply an effective ABC inequality rigorously, we first factor out the greatest common divisor

g=gcd⁡(p2,k​q2,d),\Large g=\gcd(p^{2},kq^{2},d),

and define the coprime triple

(a′,b′,c′):=(p2g,k​q2g,dg)∈ℤ3.\Large(a^{\prime},b^{\prime},c^{\prime}):=\left(\frac{p^{2}}{g},\frac{kq^{2}}{g},\frac{d}{g}\right)\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}.

Then the effective ABC conjecture yields

a′≤Kε​Rad​(a′​b′​c′​k)1+ε.\Large a^{\prime}\leq K_{\varepsilon}\,\mathrm{Rad}(a^{\prime}b^{\prime}c^{\prime}k)^{1+\varepsilon}.

Substituting back, we get

p2g≤Kε​Rad​(p2g⋅k​q2g⋅dg⋅k)1+ε.\Large\frac{p^{2}}{g}\leq K_{\varepsilon}\,\mathrm{Rad}\Big(\frac{p^{2}}{g}\cdot\frac{kq^{2}}{g}\cdot\frac{d}{g}\cdot k\Big)^{1+\varepsilon}.

Since q∈ℤSq\in\mathbb{Z}_{S}, the radical of qq is bounded by qq, and d≤(p+q​k)​|a−p/q|​q≤2​q1−ε​(p+q​k)d\leq(p+q\sqrt{k})\,|a-p/q|q\leq 2q^{1-\varepsilon}(p+q\sqrt{k}). Using these estimates, we obtain

p2−(1+ε)≤21+ε​Kε​k1+ε​q1+ε​(p+q​k)1+ε.\Large p^{2-(1+\varepsilon)}\leq 2^{1+\varepsilon}K_{\varepsilon}k^{1+\varepsilon}q^{1+\varepsilon}(p+q\sqrt{k})^{1+\varepsilon}.

Hence, for fixed ε>0\varepsilon>0 and effective ABC constant KεK_{\varepsilon}, the set of solutions (p,q)(p,q) is finite, and one can explicitly bound pp (and hence qq) in terms of KεK_{\varepsilon}, kk, and SS. This gives a fully explicit version of Ridout’s theorem for S-integer denominators, with rigorous coprimeness ensured via the factor gg.

2.14 Third Roots

Now we use our method from above based on the formula of Bombieri and Van der Poorten.

pn3=k​qn3+dnp_{n}^{3}=kq_{n}^{3}+d_{n}

resp

We only look at the first case here. The second is basically analogous. Here the gcd is not always 1 and a priori must be considered. But in the resulting inequality the case with gcd=1 is the critical one so we can assume that from the beginning. So in this sense we have ABC equations and get from ABC

pn3≤Kε​R​a​d​(pn​qn​dn​k)1+ε{p_{n}^{3}}\leq K_{\varepsilon}Rad(p_{n}q_{n}d_{n}k)^{1+\varepsilon}

For 3rd roots the formula (Bombieri & Van der Poorten, 1975, p.151, Theorem 3, formula (13)) by Bombieri and Van der Poorten is valid without error term due to Liouville’s theorem as given by Bombieri and Van der Poorten and their method can be used directly. For n>=4n>=4 an error term can arise and the method can not be started with the first step. This is the reason, why we restrict ourselves to 3rd roots here.

From (Bombieri & Van der Poorten, 1975, p.151, Theorem 3, formula (13)), we have the inequality

dn≤3​pn2qn​bn+1d_{n}\leq\frac{3p_{n}^{2}}{q_{n}b_{n+1}}

Using that inequality we get

pn3≤Kε​R​a​d​(pn​qn​dn​k)1+ε{p_{n}^{3}}\leq K_{\varepsilon}Rad(p_{n}q_{n}d_{n}k)^{1+\varepsilon}

pn3≤Kε​R​a​d​(qn)1+ε​(pn​dn​k)1+ε{p_{n}^{3}}\leq K_{\varepsilon}Rad(q_{n})^{1+\varepsilon}(p_{n}d_{n}k)^{1+\varepsilon}

pn3≤Kε​R​a​d​(qn)1+ε​(pn​k)1+ε​(3​pn2qn​bn+1)1+ε{p_{n}^{3}}\leq K_{\varepsilon}Rad(q_{n})^{1+\varepsilon}(p_{n}k)^{1+\varepsilon}(\frac{3p_{n}^{2}}{q_{n}b_{n+1}})^{1+\varepsilon}

And so using bn+1>=1{b_{n+1}>=1} finally

pn32​(1+ε)≤Kε​R​a​d​(qn)1+ε​k2+2​ε​(pnqn)1+ε{p_{n}^{\frac{3}{2(1+\varepsilon)}}}\leq K_{\varepsilon}Rad(q_{n})^{1+\varepsilon}k^{2+2\varepsilon}(\frac{p_{n}}{q_{n}})^{1+\varepsilon}

for the pnp_{n} and so the number of solutions must be finite and an explicit bound can be given as pnqn\frac{p_{n}}{q_{n}} converges to the 3rd root of k. So one choice is

pn≤(Kε​R​a​d​(qn)1+ε​k2+2​ε​(p1q1)1+ε)2​(1+ε)3p_{n}\leq(K_{\varepsilon}Rad(q_{n})^{1+\varepsilon}k^{2+2\varepsilon}(\frac{p_{1}}{q_{1}})^{1+\varepsilon})^{\frac{2({1+\varepsilon})}{3}}

2.15 Bounds for the approximation gain of ABC hits from resulting equations

Definition 2.5.

A triple of coprime integers a+b=ca+b=c is an ABC hit, if r​a​d​(a​b​c)<crad(abc)<c holds and the quality of a triple is given by the first q​u​a​l​i​t​y​(a,b,c)=l​n​(c)l​n​(r​a​d​(a​b​c))quality(a,b,c)=\frac{ln(c)}{ln(rad(abc))}. As c>1c>1 it is clear that abc is larger than 1.

2+109⋅95=2352+109\cdot 9^{5}=23^{5} is the ABC hit with the highest quality so far found. Its quality is approximately 1.62991. This hit results from the 3rd convergent to 1095\sqrt[5]{109} with regular continued fraction [2;1,1,4,77733,…][2;1,1,4,77733,\ldots]. The fraction 239\frac{23}{9} is a good approximation because 77733 is very large and very near the absolute Liouville bound.

Definition 2.6.

Let dn​qn​k​pnd_{n}q_{n}kp_{n} come from a resulting equation of ks\sqrt[s]{k}. The approximation gain of (a,b,c) equals l​n​(qns​k)l​n​(dn​qn​k​pn)\frac{ln({q_{n}}^{s}k)}{ln(d_{n}q_{n}kp_{n})} if dn>0d_{n}>0, and l​n​(pns)l​n​(−dn​qn​k​pn)\frac{ln({p_{n}}^{s})}{ln(-d_{n}q_{n}kp_{n})} if dn<0d_{n}<0.

The approximation gain is always smaller or equal to the quality.

Theorem 2.7 (Uniform bound for approximation gain for k≥3k\geq 3).

Let k≥3k\geq 3 and let α=k3\alpha=\sqrt[3]{k}. For all resulting equations arising from convergents pnqn\frac{p_{n}}{q_{n}} to α\alpha, the approximation gain satisfies

approximation gain<32.\Large\text{approximation gain}<\frac{3}{2}.
Proof.

Let pnqn\frac{p_{n}}{q_{n}} be a convergent to α=k3\alpha=\sqrt[3]{k} with resulting equation

pn3=k​qn3+dn,dn>0.\Large p_{n}^{3}=kq_{n}^{3}+d_{n},\hskip 28.80008ptd_{n}>0.

(The case dn<0d_{n}<0 is analogous.)

By Bombieri–van der Poorten (Bombieri & Van der Poorten, 1975, p. 151, Theorem 3, formula (13)), we have

dn≥3​pn2qn​(bn+1+2).\Large d_{n}\geq\frac{3p_{n}^{2}}{q_{n}(b_{n+1}+2)}.

By Liouville’s bound for cubic irrationals,

bn+1≤3​k​qn.\Large b_{n+1}\leq 3kq_{n}.

Hence

dn​qn​k​pn≥3​k​pn33​k​qn+2.\Large d_{n}q_{n}kp_{n}\geq\frac{3kp_{n}^{3}}{3kq_{n}+2}.

The approximation gain is therefore bounded by

approximation gain=ln⁡(pn3)ln⁡(dn​qn​k​pn)≤3​ln⁡pnln⁡(3​k​pn33​k​qn+2).\Large\text{approximation gain}=\frac{\ln(p_{n}^{3})}{\ln(d_{n}q_{n}kp_{n})}\leq\frac{3\ln p_{n}}{\ln\!\left(\frac{3kp_{n}^{3}}{3kq_{n}+2}\right)}.

We estimate the denominator:

ln⁡(3​k​pn33​k​qn+2)=2​ln⁡pn+ln⁡(pnqn)+ln⁡(3​k​qn3​k​qn+2).\Large\ln\!\left(\frac{3kp_{n}^{3}}{3kq_{n}+2}\right)=2\ln p_{n}+\ln\!\left(\frac{p_{n}}{q_{n}}\right)+\ln\!\left(\frac{3kq_{n}}{3kq_{n}+2}\right).

Since pnqn→α\frac{p_{n}}{q_{n}}\to\alpha and k≥3k\geq 3, we have

ln⁡(pnqn)≥ln⁡(α)≥13​ln⁡3,\Large\ln\!\left(\frac{p_{n}}{q_{n}}\right)\geq\ln(\alpha)\geq\frac{1}{3}\ln 3,

while

ln⁡(3​k​qn3​k​qn+2)≥−23​k​qn≥−29.\Large\ln\!\left(\frac{3kq_{n}}{3kq_{n}+2}\right)\geq-\frac{2}{3kq_{n}}\geq-\frac{2}{9}.

Combining these estimates yields

ln⁡(3​k​pn33​k​qn+2)>2​ln⁡pnfor all ​n.\Large\ln\!\left(\frac{3kp_{n}^{3}}{3kq_{n}+2}\right)>2\ln p_{n}\hskip 14.40004pt\text{for all }n.

Consequently,

approximation gain<3​ln⁡pn2​ln⁡pn=32,\Large\text{approximation gain}<\frac{3\ln p_{n}}{2\ln p_{n}}=\frac{3}{2},

which proves the theorem. ∎

Theorem 2.8.

Now The case k=2k=2. Let α=23\alpha=\sqrt[3]{2}. For all resulting equations arising from convergents pnqn\frac{p_{n}}{q_{n}} to α\alpha, the approximation gain satisfies

approximation gain<32.\Large\text{approximation gain}<\frac{3}{2}.
Proof.

Let pnqn\frac{p_{n}}{q_{n}} be a convergent to α=23\alpha=\sqrt[3]{2} with resulting equation

pn3=2​qn3+dn.\Large p_{n}^{3}=2q_{n}^{3}+d_{n}.

As in the proof of Theorem 2.8, Bombieri–van der Poorten and Liouville’s bound imply

approximation gain≤3​ln⁡pn2​ln⁡pn+ln⁡(α)+o⁡(1).\Large\text{approximation gain}\leq\frac{3\ln p_{n}}{2\ln p_{n}+\ln(\alpha)+o(1)}.

Since ln⁡(α)>0\ln(\alpha)>0, it follows that

limn→∞approximation gain=32,\Large\lim_{n\to\infty}\text{approximation gain}=\frac{3}{2},

and the limit is approached from below. Consequently, there exists an index NN such that

approximation gain<32for all ​n≥N.\Large\text{approximation gain}<\frac{3}{2}\hskip 14.40004pt\text{for all }n\geq N.

It therefore suffices to verify the inequality for the finitely many indices n<Nn<N.

The first convergent is p1q1=43\frac{p_{1}}{q_{1}}=\frac{4}{3}, which yields

p13−2​q13=64−54=10,\Large p_{1}^{3}-2q_{1}^{3}=64-54=10,

and hence

approximation gain=ln⁡(64)ln⁡(4⋅3⋅10)<32.\Large\text{approximation gain}=\frac{\ln(64)}{\ln(4\cdot 3\cdot 10)}<\frac{3}{2}.

A direct computation of the remaining convergents with n<Nn<N confirms that

approximation gain<32\Large\text{approximation gain}<\frac{3}{2}

in each case. This completes the proof. ∎

2.16 General case if the formula can be used

When it is assumed that the method of Bombieri and Van der Poorten works as well for km\sqrt[m]{k} with m≥3m\geq 3 and k≥2k\geq 2 then the following would result:

The inequality of Bombieri and Van der Poorten is dn≥m​pnm−1qn​(bn+1+2)d_{n}\geq\frac{mp_{n}^{m-1}}{q_{n}(b_{n+1}+2)}

Liouville’s bound is bn+1≤m​k​qnb_{n+1}\leq mkq_{n}

And the resulting inequality is

approximation gain = l​n​(pnm)l​n​(dn​qn​k​pn)≤\frac{ln({p_{n}}^{m})}{ln(d_{n}q_{n}kp_{n})}\leq m2\frac{m}{2}

So even when it would work (the error terms can be ignored and the algorithm started, which is clear for 3rd degree) the bound for this inequality would diverge and so no universal bound for all m can be found on this road as Liouville’s bound is not strong enough for this purpose.

So the ABC gains can be seperated for resulting equation in approximation gains and power gains. The approximation gain can be bounded by 32\frac{3}{2} for 3rd roots. To prove a bound for the quality the power gains l​n​(pn​qn​dn​k)l​n​(r​a​d​(dn​qn​k​pn))\frac{ln({p_{n}q_{n}d_{n}k})}{ln(rad(d_{n}q_{n}kp_{n}))} must be bounded as well, which seems to be very difficult even for special cases like 23\sqrt[3]{2} (remarkable are here the second equation 128 = 125 + 3 with a power gain of 1.4 and an approximation gain of 1.01 and the 5th equation with a power gain of 1.37 and an approximation gain of 0.99).

To bound the power gains a strong explicit effective ABC result is needed. There is a discussion in the mathematical community, if Mochizuki’s results can be used. We do not know this, but if they can be used the following follows:

Theorem 2.9 (Explicit ABC).

For every positive real number ε\varepsilon, there exists a constant LεL_{\varepsilon} such that for all triples (a,b,c)(a,b,c) of coprime positive integers, with a+b=ca+b=c:

c<Lε⋅r​a​d​(a​b​c)3+ε.\Large c<L_{\varepsilon}\cdot rad(abc)^{3+\varepsilon}.

This can be used to prove that the power gains of the quality for resulting ABC equations of 3rd roots are bounded for a fixed k:

power gain = l​n​(pn​qn​dn​k)l​n​(r​a​d​(dn​qn​k​pn))\frac{ln({p_{n}q_{n}d_{n}k})}{ln(rad(d_{n}q_{n}kp_{n}))}

≤l​n​(k2​pn3)l​n​(r​a​d​(dn​qn​k​pn))\leq\frac{ln({k}^{2}{p_{n}}^{3})}{ln(rad(d_{n}q_{n}kp_{n}))}

using the formula (Bombieri & Van der Poorten, 1975, p.151, Theorem 3, formula (13)) by Bombieri and Van der Poorten and the fact that bn+1>=1b_{n+1}>=1.

= l​n​(k2​pn3)l​n​((r​a​d​(dn​qn​k​pn)3+ε)13+ε)\frac{ln({k}^{2}{p_{n}}^{3})}{ln((rad(d_{n}q_{n}kp_{n})^{3+\varepsilon})^{\frac{1}{3+\varepsilon}})}

≤l​n​(k2​pn3)l​n​(pn3Lε13+ε)\leq\frac{ln({k}^{2}{p_{n}}^{3})}{ln(\frac{{p_{n}}^{3}}{L_{\varepsilon}}^{\frac{1}{3+\varepsilon}})}

for n large enough. This converges to 3+ε{3+\varepsilon} and is therefore bounded for all n. The bound itself depends on k and is of course extremely large.

Recently Zhou (2025) has reduced the constant LεL_{\varepsilon} from about 103010^{30} to 400 under certain extra conditions.

One concept to prove the ABC conjecture might then be to prove that both gains are bounded seperately. We conjecture that the approximation gain is bounded by 32\frac{3}{2} and the power gain by 3.
